notes.meaning: The Lord told Moses to command Aaron's sons, the priests, not to make themselves ritually unclean by touching or being near a dead body. In the ancient world, death was a reminder of decay and sin, and coming near a corpse barred a person from public worship for seven days. Because priests were called to minister to the living God every day, they could not routinely step away from their duties for ordinary funerals.

God allowed an exception when a death occurred within the priest's closest circle of blood relatives. A priest could mourn and help bury his parents, children, brother, or an unmarried sister who still lived in his household. Ancient interpreters also understood this to include his wife, since husband and wife are joined as one flesh. In this way, God honored natural family love and made room for human grief.

An ordinary priest was forbidden to defile himself for distant relatives, in-laws, or other members of his community. As a leader among God's people, he could not compromise his sacred standing or neglect the sanctuary for general mourning. His calling required him to keep God's work first.

Priests were strictly forbidden from copying the pagan mourning rituals of nearby nations, such as shaving bald patches on their heads, trimming their beards, or cutting their skin. Heathen peoples practiced these painful customs to appease false gods or show wild despair. God's ministers were called to show calm trust and patient hope even in times of deep loss.

Priests had to be entirely dedicated to God and protect His holy name from dishonor. They placed the sacrifices on the altar, which scripture calls the food of God to picture warm table-fellowship between the Lord and His people. Handling these sacred offerings required them to live clean, obedient lives at all times.

An ordinary priest was not allowed to marry a woman who had worked as a prostitute, had an unchaste reputation, or had been divorced. His home life was to reflect the same honor and purity as his public ministry, preventing any scandal from damaging God's worship. He was free to marry a godly virgin or an upright widow.

The people of Israel were instructed to treat the priest with great reverence because he handled the holy offerings before God. The nation had a shared duty to protect the honor of the priesthood and ensure these marriage laws were kept. Believers today are likewise called to hold faithful spiritual leaders in high esteem for their work's sake.

If a priest's daughter became a prostitute, she brought shame not only upon herself but upon her father and his sacred office. Because she grew up enjoying the privileges of a holy household, her offense was treated with severe judgment, ending in death by burning. A leader's family is called to be an example of godliness rather than a cause of reproach.

The high priest held the highest position among the priests, marked by the pouring of special anointing oil on his head and by wearing the holy vestments. He was forbidden from letting his hair go uncombed or tearing his clothes as signs of grief. His role as the chief intercessor between God and the nation demanded unbroken dignity and self-control.

The high priest was barred from entering any house where a corpse lay, even for his own mother or father. While other priests had family exceptions, the high priest could never allow ritual uncleanness to pause his mediation for the nation. His duty to the living God took priority over the most tender earthly relationships.

The high priest was forbidden to leave his sacred post in the sanctuary to attend a funeral, which would defile God's holy dwelling place. The consecration of the holy anointing oil—meaning he was completely set apart for God—rested upon him. His constant service pointed forward to Jesus Christ, who lives forever to intercede for His people.

The high priest was held to even stricter marriage requirements than the other priests, being permitted to marry only an Israelite virgin. He could not marry a widow, a divorced woman, or any woman with a compromised reputation. This kept his family line pure and served as a living picture of the church presented to Christ as a pure and spotless bride.

By marrying properly, the high priest ensured that his children were respected and qualified to inherit the holy office. An improper marriage would bring disgrace on his family line and unfit his sons for sacred service. The Lord, who sanctified the priest—meaning He set him apart as holy—expected the priest's home to honor that calling.

God gave Moses rules about the descendants of Aaron who had physical defects, barring them from stepping forward to offer sacrifices. While a physical defect was not a moral fault or a sin, the altar required external wholeness to show the supreme perfection of God. This outward standard foreshadowed Jesus Christ, the spotless High Priest who offered Himself without defect.

The text lists specific physical conditions that disqualified a priest from officiating, including blindness, lameness, facial disfigurement, limb deformities, hunchbacks, severe wasting, eye defects, chronic skin conditions, or crushed testicles. A man with any of these conditions could not carry out public duties at the altar. These visible requirements preserved the dignity of the sanctuary and kept the worship from human distraction or disrespect.

The Lord repeated the main rule that no son of Aaron with a bodily blemish could approach to offer the fire-offerings. Repeating the command showed how essential it was for Israel to keep worship strictly according to God's pattern. It taught that anyone who represents sinners before God must be whole and complete.

Even though a blemished priest was barred from serving at the altar, God graciously provided for his daily needs by allowing him to eat the sacred food. He received his full share of both the holy portions, like tithes, and the most holy portions, like meat from the sin offerings. God showed that an involuntary physical limitation never cut a person off from His loving care and provision.

The priest with a blemish could not enter the Holy Place behind the curtain to trim lamps or burn incense, nor could he approach the altar outside. Barring him from these duties protected God's holy dwelling places from being treated as ordinary. This rule reminded worshippers that fallen, imperfect humanity cannot step into God's presence without a perfect mediator.

Moses shared every detail of these laws with Aaron, his sons, and the entire congregation of Israel. Because the priests served on behalf of the whole nation, every Israelite needed to understand the rules and help hold the priesthood accountable. God's plan for holy worship was made plain for the whole community to know and protect.
